Posted October 31, 2004
Analysis by Richard Cowan Sponsored by Advanced Nutrients.

It is only a coincidence however ominous and unwelcome that the Canadian Supreme Court unanimously ruled last week that the police could use infrared cameras in their search for indoor grow ops. In any case, regardless of the philosophical questions, the political reality is that the Canadian police are grabbing for more power, and Health Canada is up to its old tricks again.

Meanwhile, the weak minority government will be bringing its phony decrim bill back to the Parliament, perhaps this week.
See
 Cannabis Reform and The Canadian Election. (It's Okay to Exhale, and I Promise that Your Eyes Won't Glaze Over.)

Also, at the urging of the police bureaucracy, both the BC and Ontario legislatures are likely to pass civil forfeiture laws that will be abused just as they were in DEAland. In fact, this has been in the works for a long time, but the Canadian politicians have as usual learned all the wrong lessons from south of their border.
From 2000 see
 As DEAland Begins to Move Away from " Civil Forfeiture " Ontario and the UK Start Down A Very Dangerous Path. -- 3 Articles
For more on DEAland forfeiture laws, see www.fear.org

On the other hand, the Canadian Supreme Court did also reaffirm their 5-2 split decision in July that Canadian police cannot go on fishing expeditions searching people for evidence simply because they suspect someone.

The Supremes overruled the Manitoba Court of Appeal and said that Winnipeg police had no right to search the pockets of a man in December 2000. As it happens, the case involved cannabis possession. The police found 27.5 grams roughly an ounce of cannabis, but the evidence was disallowed on the grounds it was illegally obtained. It is also interesting to note that having one ounce of cannabis became the basis of a trafficking charge.
See
 What Is It About War That You Don't Understand? Charging Marc Emery With Trafficking Was No Accident, And Neither Was The Wording Of The Law.

Individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their pockets, Justice Frank Iacobucci wrote for the majority.

The search here went beyond what was required to mitigate concerns about officer safety and reflects a serious breach of (the defendant's) protection against unreasonable search and seizure.

In fact, these two rulings set the stage for the Canadian government's pretense that they will provide greater tolerance for possession, but harsher penalties for growing and selling.

Unfortunately, Health Canada continues to defy both common sense and common decency. On Tuesday, Canadians for Safe Access issued the following press release:

New Health Canada Medicinal Cannabis Regulations Put Demands of Police Over Needs of Patients

Health Canada's Office of Cannabis Medical Access (OCMA) has once again placed the demands of police over the needs of patients suffering from critical and chronic illnesses.
From 2000 see
 Health Canada Press Release Makes Clear that the Health of Canadians Is Less Important than Marijuana Prohibition. Victimization of a Patient Gives More Proof.
and
 Health Canada Gives $5.7 Million Contract to Company With No Experience to Grow Mediocre Weed for Medical Marijuana Research

The latest set of amendments includes a plan to eventually phase out the option of personal production in favour of the pharmacy-based distribution of the government's own poor quality and potentially unsafe product.

The inadequacy of Health Canada's product is evident: currently only 74 out of the 753 patients enrolled in the Marijuana Medical Access Regulations program purchase their cannabis from Health Canada, said Philippe Lucas of Canadians for Safe Access. He added that nearly 30% of the 93 people who originally ordered the PPS cannabis returned it to the government. Health Canada continues to implement policies designed to entrench its monopoly on production and to placate police demands, rather than addressing the real and immediate needs and concerns of medical users, said Lucas.
See
 Hypocrisy and Democracy: Raid on Medical Cannabis Research Facility Critical of Health Canada's Schwag Challenges Canada's Values. What Will The Politicians Say?

Most MMAR license holders attain their supply through personal cultivation or access through compassion clubs and societies. Compassion clubs currently help over 8000 critically and chronically ill Canadians, including over half (400+) of the OCMA exemptees; all at no cost to the taxpayer. Lucas questions why Health Canada is ignoring or eliminating these options for safe access to medicine. Our nation's critically and chronically ill are not children that need to be protected from themselves or from medicinal cannabis; they are sick and suffering and deserve the strongest and safest medicine right now.

The OCMA's new regulations necessitate the recommendation of a specialist for most applicants to gain access to the program, despite Health Canada's own acknowledgement that for many Canadians this is a major and often insurmountable hurdle. This policy contradicts the stated intention of opening up access to a program that has actually seen a steady reduction in the rate of applications since its peak in April of 2002, said Lucas. According to Health Canada statistics, the number of participants in the program actually decreased by 28 people between July and September of this year, demonstrating that access has actually not been improved at all.

Politically, this looks slightly different in DEAland, where the government is still pretending that medical cannabis is just a plot by evil legalizers to put crack vending machines in nursery schools. Consequently, NORML's latest weekly press release was slightly ambivalent:

New Health Canada Regulations Authorize Cannabis Sales In Pharmacies

Ottawa, Ontario: Regulations announced by Health Canada this week " provide limited authority for a pharmacy-based distribution system for dried marijuana that is produced by a [government] licensed dealer. "

The new regulations, first proposed in March, encourage federal authorities to develop a protocol to allow for pharmacies to provide medical cannabis to qualified patients. The proposed plan is modeled after a one-year-old Dutch program that authorizes the sale and distribution of government-approved pot by prescription in licensed pharmacies.

" Involving pharmacists in the distribution system could enhance the identification and mitigation of risks to the authorized person, particularly when marijuana is combined with other drug therapies the authorized person may be using, " the regulations state. " Stakeholders have expressed strong support for the conduct of a pilot project to assess the feasibility of distributing marijuana for medical purposes through a pharmacy-based system. This alternative provides the authority to enable such a pilot project to take place. "
See
 Health Canada's Office of Cannabis Medical Access' Stakeholder Advisory Committee Includes Physicians for A Smoke Free Canada - Not The Compassion Societies. But It Will Let Them Talk For An Hour

NORML Foundation Executive Director Allen St. Pierre said that a regulated distribution program is appropriate. " If we are to hold cannabis up to the same standards of safety and efficacy that we hold other drugs, then Health Canada should implement a policy so patients may obtain it legally without subjecting themselves to the risks inherent to the black market. "

Under Canadian law, authorized patients may grow cannabis for medical purposes, or purchase government-grown marijuana from Health Canada. However, of the 781 Canadians licensed with Health Canada to use medical marijuana legally, fewer than 100 have opted to acquire federal pot because of its alleged poor quality. As a result, half of the country's qualified patients obtain medicinal cannabis from patient cooperatives, so-called " compassion clubs, " which cultivate and provide medical-grade pot to patients at a minimal cost.

In an October 2003 Ontario Court of Appeals ruling, Health Canada was ordered to immediately amend its regulations to allow for the licensing of such cooperatives, though the agency has yet to do so. Health Canada made no mention of the role " compassion clubs " play in the distribution of medicinal cannabis in its amended regulations, causing some Canadian patients to question the agency's motives.

" The latest set of amendments includes a plan to eventually phase out the option of personal [cannabis] production in favor of the pharmacy-based distribution of the government's own poor quality and potentially unsafe product, " said Philippe Lucas of Canadians for Safe Access. " Health Canada continues to implement policies designed to entrench its monopoly on [marijuana] production and to placate police demands, rather than addressing the real and immediate needs and concerns of medical users. "

For more information, please contact Allen St. Pierre, Executive Director of the NORML Foundation, at (202) 483-5500. Full text of the new Health

Canada regulations are available online at: http://canadagazette.gc.ca/partI/2004/20041023/html/regle2-e.html

Of course, NORML is in favor of the complete legalization of cannabis, so there is no real philosophical disagreement with Canadians for Safe Access. Rather, from the American perspective, the prospect of HC trying to put medical cannabis into pharmacies while John Walters and his little band of sociopaths are busy lying about the IOM report is simply irresistible.
See
 Bush's New Freedom Initiative: Treatment For Using Cannabis, From The Wonderful Folks Who Brought Us Vioxx, Baycol, Etc. Author of IOM Report Says, " I can't understand why it isn't rescheduled. "

Ironically, HC's biggest problem in implementing a pharmacy based distribution system will continue to be its own ironclad commitment to ignorance about cannabis.
See
 Canadian Health Minister Seeks Asylum In DEAland; Says Making Her Think About Medical Cannabis Constitutes Torture. In DC They Don't Allow That Sort of Thing. Thinking, That Is.

Ignorance about cannabis necessarily involves a commitment to ignorance about The Netherlands, and the Dutch project for distributing medical cannabis in pharmacies is foundering because it cannot compete with the coffeeshops.
See
 MarijuanaNews Reported It A Month Ago, But Now It's Official: Dutch Pharmacies Provide Medical cannabis Covered by Health Insurance.

James Burton, an American who moved to Holland many years ago after suffering a year in prison for growing his own cannabis to fight glaucoma, was one of two licensed growers for the government program. In 2001 he signed a contract to provide the Dutch government with medical grade cannabis.

Unlike Canada's authorized grower, Burton really knew what he was doing. In the early 90s, he founded the Stichting (Foundation) Institute of Medical Marijuana in Rotterdam, and for over ten years he sold medical cannabis to as many as 1,500 patients. So, it was logical that he would be chosen to grow for the Office of Medicinal Cannabis, a part of the Dutch Ministry of Health.

Unfortunately, his five-year contract was cancelled last month because he talked about it on Dutch television and was accused by the government of violating a confidentiality clause. He said that he had to complain. Burton told the Associated Press, I finally had to come out publicly. The program's not working. They have less than 1,000 patients.

Burton blamed the center-right government for not promoting the program, but it seems unlikely that any government program could compete with the variety and quality of the cannabis sold in the hundreds of coffeeshops around the country, especially since some of the shops give discounts to patients.

Thus, developments in Holland also lend support for the arguments advanced by Philippe Lucas and Canadians for Safe Access. Even the Dutch government could not properly address the needs of medical cannabis users. But Health Canada really is not trying.

Thus far, HC has gotten away with repeatedly ignoring various court rulings supporting the rights of patients to have real access to real medical cannabis. The Ontario Court of Appeals even reinstated the federal prohibition after effectively rewriting the laws. Unfortunately, the Canadian courts have not been very effective in supporting their own rulings.

There are now several cases pending before the courts in British Columbia that could threaten all of cannabis prohibition again. Philippe Lucas has a civil case in the works. The Kubbys will be announcing their own challenge soon (and they need and deserve some support in this effort). Moreover, it is likely that some of criminal cases will involve a defense based on the fact that HC continues to violate the rights of patients.

The stage is set for a variety of challenges to cannabis prohibition in the friendly venues of the BC courts.

The BC courts have already shown that they are committed to the concept of medical cannabis, and they will also have had the advantage of seeing HC's wretched track record. Consequently, it is quite possible that the BC courts will toss out all of the cannabis laws because there is simply no way that the needs of patients can be reconciled with police/organized crime control over the cannabis supply.
From 2001, see
 Is Health Canada's Medical Marijuana Fiasco A Time Bomb Ticking Under Canadian Prohibition?

In any case, it is clear that the war on cannabis will be escalating in the months ahead.
